items.title: Enterprise Data Product Architecture Framework
items.abstract: Modern enterprises are shifting from project-centric data pipelines toward reusable data products that are owned, governed, discoverable, and consumed through standardized interfaces. This transformation requires an architecture that connects business domains, semantic models, data contracts, quality, lineage, metadata, security, interoperability, observability, lifecycle governance, and measurable value. This paper proposes an Enterprise Data Product Architecture Framework that defines the structural and operating principles required to design and manage data products across SAP and non-SAP landscapes. The framework integrates SAP Business Data Cloud, SAP Datasphere, SAP HANA Cloud, APIs, event-driven integration, metadata catalogs, data quality services, data sharing, analytics, and AI consumption. It establishes product roles, architecture layers, data contracts, governance controls, service levels, lifecycle stages, and KPIs/KRIs. The proposed approach enables organizations to reduce duplication, improve trust and reuse, accelerate analytics and Artificial Intelligence, and strengthen business accountability for enterprise data.

items.title: Enterprise Multi-Agent Architecture Framework
items.abstract: Enterprises are rapidly moving from isolated copilots toward ecosystems of specialized AI agents that collaborate across business processes, data domains, applications, and cloud platforms. Multi-agent systems can improve decomposition, parallel execution, specialization, resilience, and decision quality, but they also introduce architectural challenges involving identity, delegation, shared memory, tool access, message routing, conflict resolution, security, observability, and accountability. This paper proposes an Enterprise Multi-Agent Architecture Framework that defines a layered architecture for agent discovery, orchestration, inter-agent communication, knowledge grounding, enterprise integration, policy enforcement, runtime isolation, and human oversight. The framework combines enterprise architecture principles, Zero Trust, Responsible AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Knowledge Graphs, API governance, event-driven integration, and lifecycle management. It enables organizations to design scalable multi-agent environments in which specialized agents can collaborate safely while maintaining traceability, bounded authority, data protection, and measurable business outcomes across hybrid and multi-cloud landscapes.

items.title: Epileptic seizure onset early warning using a lightweight multimodal self-explainable neural network
items.abstract: BackgroundCutting-edge deep learning algorithms are applied to epileptic seizures to uncover hidden patterns and achieve high accuracy. Post hoc algorithms explain black-box models but do not reveal the detailed workings of the algorithms. Therefore, intrinsic methods overcome these issues; however, they suffer from improper use of indicative metrics and performance-to-accuracy trade-offs.ObjectiveThis study implements a lightweight multimodal explainable Neural Network for real-time early warning of epileptic seizure onset.MethodsPeople with drug-resistant epilepsy across all age groups who had regular follow-up at Emanuel Mental Specialized Hospital in Ethiopia during the data collection period were the study population. EEG recordings were performed using the 10/20 system. A pretest was conducted two weeks before actual data collection. EDFbrowser was used for preparing the dataset in CSV format. Learned and identity self-explainable neural network algorithms were used to develop a model. In addition to classical evaluation metrics, explicitness, faithfulness, stability, and clear patterns behind predictions were used. Ethical approval was also obtained from the institutional review board (IRB) with reference number No: AM/146/2/36.ResultsLearned and identity self-explainable neural networks were developed and compared. The models' accuracies are 96.524% and 95.328%, and their stability mean values are 99.88% and 99.88%, respectively. Additionally, explicitness values of 0.0055 and 0.01197 were achieved, respectively.ConclusionThe results demonstrate that using a self-explainable neural network is a promising step toward responsible and transparent artificial intelligence. Comparing the two models shows that the learned self-explainable neural network is slightly more optimistic than the identity self-explainable neural network.

items.title: Epilogue
items.abstract: Chapter 8 introduces the concept of the vocation economy, extending the original framework of the author’s first book of this trilogy, On Vocation – How to Align Your Purpose with Your Profession , from the inner journey of individuals to the broader dynamics of organisations, markets and societal systems. It argues that vocation is no longer merely a personal search for meaning but an emerging organising principle for institutions operating in an age of technological acceleration, social disruption and growing demand for authenticity. As individuals seek alignment between their values and their work, organisations are increasingly challenged to embed purpose into their strategy, culture and governance. When personal vocation and organisational purpose diverge, disengagement, mistrust and institutional fragility follow. Drawing on the author’s professional experiences and insights from thinkers such as Viktor Frankl, Peter Drucker, Amartya Sen and Mariana Mazzucato, the chapter frames vocation as a systemic force shaping the future of work and economic life. It explores how talent, capital and innovation increasingly flow towards institutions that demonstrate coherence between purpose and practice. At the same time, emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence amplify the ethical stakes of this transformation, making it essential that technological progress remains anchored in human dignity and accountability. Ultimately, the chapter positions the vocation economy as the next evolutionary stage of capitalism – one defined by alignment between individuals, organisations and societal needs – where purpose becomes the foundation of resilience, trust and long-term flourishing.

items.title: Equipping the next generation: addressing the unmet need for artificial intelligence education at research performing organizations
items.abstract: Abstract Background The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools into higher education is rapidly accelerating, yet the educational ecosystem appears largely unprepared for the scale and speed of adoption. Our recent international survey of over 1,200 university students and postdoctoral fellows in the medical and life sciences found that while more than 80% had used GenAI tools, the vast majority had received no formal training, and many were unaware of any institutional policies governing their use. This gap between adoption and institutional preparedness may pose risks to research integrity if left unaddressed. Main body Existing research supports a coordinated, evidence-informed approach to AI education in research performing organizations (RPOs), grounded in principles of research integrity, equity, and critical engagement with technology. First, GenAI literacy must be embedded as a core competency in scientific and clinical education, equipping students to critically evaluate tool outputs, recognize hallucination and bias, and understand the distinction between AI-generated inaccuracy and deliberate research misconduct. Second, traditional frameworks for academic integrity would benefit from re-examination. Today, GenAI tools have fundamentally disrupted established notions of authorship, originality, and plagiarism, and the absence of coherent institutional guidance leaves students and educators navigating these questions without support. Third, RPOs must develop clear, transparent, and context-sensitive policies on GenAI use by embedding responsible AI education into curricula, equipping learners not only to use these tools effectively, but to question, verify, and critique their outputs in ways that uphold scientific standards. Conclusion RPOs have an urgent responsibility to move beyond reactive responses and toward proactive strategies that uphold scientific standards, promote equity of access, and prepare the next generation of researchers and clinicians to engage with GenAI responsibly and ethically.

items.title: Ethical AI and Responsible Data Use in Education
items.abstract: This chapter introduces the concept of personalised learning, learning analytics, automated assessment, and the emergence of generative AI in transforming education, while also highlighting the ethical, privacy, governance and cybersecurity dilemmas that arise with implementation of Artificial Intelligence in the education sector. The chapter gives an overview of ethical and responsible use of AI in education, starting with an examination of the educational AI ecosystem, followed by a discussion of data lifecycle in education, and concluding with an exploration of algorithmic bias, transparency, informed consent, data ownership, surveillance and risks posed by generative AI. It outlines the principles of responsible data governance, privacy-by-design, privacy-preserving methods and other international frameworks like GDPR AI Ethics and OECD Principles. The topics of AI-driven cybersecurity, key practice insights for both educators and institutions, developers and policymakers, and future research areas for AI are also discussed.

items.title: Ethical leadership and job crafting: the role of intrinsic motivation and job feedback
items.abstract: Introduction Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and its sub-theory Cognitive Evaluation Theory (CET), the present study examines how ethical leadership relates to employees’ job crafting through intrinsic motivation, and how this indirect relationship is contingent on job feedback. We proposed that ethical leadership is positively related to job crafting via intrinsic motivation, and that job feedback moderates this indirect effect by providing competence-relevant informational cues. Methods We tested our hypotheses using two-wave data collected from 102 employees in the customer service department of a gaming company in northern China. Results The results provided preliminary evidence of a moderated mediation pattern, suggesting that the indirect association between ethical leadership and job crafting through intrinsic motivation varied as a function of job feedback. Discussion These findings extend research on ethical leadership and job crafting by clarifying intrinsic motivation as the motivational mechanism and job feedback as a key boundary condition. The theoretical and practical implications are discussed.

items.title: Ethical Policies for Generative Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education
items.abstract: The use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education requires frameworks that promote its responsible, flexible, transparent, and academically rigorous use. This paper first provides a literature review of the current state of the art on the ethical use of GenAI in higher education between 2023 and 2025. The aim is to examine how higher education institutions, researchers, and educators have responded to the ethical challenges associated with integrating GenAI into teaching and learning. It then presents a descriptive and analytical study of the Russell Group's principles for the use of GenAI in higher education (2023)—transparency, equity, reliability, accountability, and autonomy—and analyses the information published on the websites of its twenty-four member universities. This analysis makes it possible to determine the extent to which similar regulatory principles have been adopted by other institutions and to evaluate the benefits of establishing clear policies and procedures to support a transparent and effective academic framework.

items.title: Ethics of AI and Non-Human Entities
items.abstract: This paper examines the ethical and philosophical implications of the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technology—not for human society, but for “non-human beings” and the Earth’s ecosystems.Conventional discussions of AI ethics and the philosophy of technology have consistently remained within an “anthropocentric” framework focused on human labor, copyright, or whether AI possesses a mind equivalent to that of humans.However, modern AI is already deeply penetrating the natural world.In this paper, from the perspectives of environmental philosophy and bioethics, we present three core paradigms: I) the redefinition of the dignity of life brought about by the translation of animal language using AI; II) signal pollution in the natural world caused by digital technology (ecological deepfakes); and III) the environmental burden and infringement on the right to life of other organisms resulting from the materiality of computation.In conclusion, we argue that future AI ethics must undergo a paradigm shift toward “Environmental AI Ethics,” which encompasses all life systems beyond humans. items.title: Evaluating AI-Powered Tools for English Lesson Plan Generation
items.abstract: The aim of this study was to compare the effectiveness, pedagogical quality, and user experience of ChatGPT and two AI-powered educational tools, Magicschool.ai and Eduaide.ai, in generating lesson plans for teaching English as a Foreign Language (EFL). The analysis examined the extent to which the generated lesson plans align with modern pedagogical principles, demonstrate usability, clarity and adaptability, and address key EFL instructional needs, including grammar accuracy, vocabulary development, student engagement, and classroom practicality. For each tool, two different prompts were used to produce distinct lesson plans, which were subsequently evaluated by the researcher in terms of quality and instructional efficiency. The comparative analysis indicates that all three AI-platforms demonstrate pedagogical coherence, alignment with EFL approaches and methods. In terms of creativity, flexibility, accuracy, they do not seem to present great differences. However, they differ in their degree of practicality, differentiation, and learner's active thinking.

items.title: Evaluating ChatGPT for Dam Behavior Prediction, Interpretation, and Safety Assessment: An Experimental Study
items.abstract: Structural dam safety control is fundamentally based on visual inspections and on the analysis of monitoring data and their comparison with the expected behavior for a given load combination, which in turn is calculated with a predictive model. In recent decades, the development of machine learning algorithms has led engineers and researchers worldwide to explore their capabilities for predicting dam behavior and supporting safety assessment. Regardless of the model used, a prediction is generally obtained together with an expected model error, which is compared with the observed value in order to support decision-making. This process, however, requires the intervention of experts in dam engineering, and particularly in the prior behavior of the structure under analysis. In recent years, the emergence of generative artificial intelligence models has opened up considerable opportunities to improve processes in various fields, including civil engineering. The reported capabilities of these models make them well suited to some tasks in the field of dam safety, particularly for developing predictive models and interpreting their results. In this work, we tested ChatGPT to assess its potential in these tasks, using the data from the ICOLD 2022 Benchmark Workshop, in which 18 teams provided their best predictions of the behavior of an arch dam. ChatGPT was provided with the same problem description and monitoring data available to the participants and was asked, through brief and neutral prompts, to propose a modeling strategy, generate predictions for six response variables for short- and long-term periods, create the corresponding source code, and interpret the results from a dam safety perspective. The complete procedure was performed twice using the same information and prompts. The results show considerable potential for increasing productivity in building and applying machine learning models, with predictive accuracy comparable to that obtained by the Benchmark participants. ChatGPT achieved a lower mean absolute error than the participants’ average in 10 (first run) and 12 (second run) of the 12 variable–period combinations, and outperformed the best participant in one case. However, the interpretation of the results was considerably weaker, with important aspects being only partially addressed or overlooked. These findings highlight the potential of ChatGPT to assist in the development of data-based predictive models, but also reveal its limitations in terms of the domain-specific knowledge required to draw conclusions on dam safety.

items.title: Evaluating LLMs for named entity recognition: a cost-benefit analysis in the legal domain
items.abstract: Abstract Within the legal domain, named entity recognition (NER) is an essential pre-processing tool for important tasks such as information extraction and redaction. Research to date has focused on rule-based approaches or machine learning strategies that require significant time and effort to train through labelled corpora. Large, multi-purpose generative large language models (LLMs) have been successfully employed on natural language processing (NLP) tasks with no prior supervised training and may represent a way forward in addressing these existing bottlenecks. Despite promising results in certain NLP use cases, the Few-Shot LLM performance on unfamiliar, domain-specific NER tasks has, to date, remained uncertain. In this legal clause NER task, we evaluate a Few-Shot, Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting strategy for OpenAI’s GPT-4 LLM on a new CUAD-NER dataset that we have repurposed for the task of Person and Organisation entity identification. In a comparative study, we demonstrate that the GPT4 + Few-Shot CoT prompt strategy outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, achieving a 5% percentage point improvement in Micro F1 score over the best performing BERT base (cased) competitor. This study also takes the novel approach of assessing the business feasibility of deploying each of these machine learning models through a detailed cost–benefit analysis that measures the trade-off between performance metrics and low and high usage running costs.

items.title: Evo-B&B: Behavior-Aware LLM-Guided Joint Evolution of Branching and Node Selection Policies for MILP
items.abstract: In branch-and-bound for Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP), branching and node selection are two critical and tightly coupled decisions, yet most existing learning-based approaches focus on optimizing them separately. We propose Evo-B&B, an LLM-guided evolutionary framework that jointly evolves executable branching and node selection policies using end-to-end SCIP solving feedback. To improve search efficiency and reduce redundant evaluations of behaviorally similar policies, Evo-B&B introduces a behavior-aware multi-island evolutionary mechanism. It measures policy similarity from branching and node-selection behaviors on a fixed set of B&B decision states and uses this similarity to preserve population diversity. We evaluate Evo-B&B on four standard MILP benchmarks across multiple instance scales. Experimental results show that Evo-B&B achieves competitive solving performance and generalizes well to larger-scale instances, while ablation studies further demonstrate the effectiveness of joint evolution and behavior-aware diversity management.

items.title: Evolution of guideline-based male infertility responses by large language models between 2025 and 2026: a comparative analysis of ChatGPT, Perplexity, and DeepSeek
items.abstract: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by patients and clinicians to obtain medical information, yet their performance may change over time as models are updated. Male infertility is a guideline-sensitive field in which inaccurate or incomplete information may affect diagnostic evaluation, counseling, and treatment expectations. This study evaluated the year-on-year evolution of ChatGPT, Perplexity, and DeepSeek in responding to guideline-derived male infertility questions between 2025 and 2026. Results A total of 528 chatbot responses were evaluated from 88 European Association of Urology (EAU) guideline-derived male infertility questions answered by ChatGPT, Perplexity, and DeepSeek in 2025 and 2026. In 2025, significant inter-model differences were observed across all four scored domains, with Perplexity achieving the highest content-quality and expert-rated scores and DeepSeek showing the weakest performance. In 2026, DISCERN scores converged across models, whereas significant differences persisted for readability, Global Quality Score, and expert opinion. ChatGPT showed significant improvement across all four scored domains and achieved the highest Global Quality Score in 2026. DeepSeek demonstrated the most pronounced improvement, particularly in DISCERN and expert opinion scores. Perplexity improved in readability but did not show a parallel positive change in Global Quality Score or expert-rated clinical usefulness. Potential patient-safety concerns were identified in seven of the 88 DeepSeek responses from 2025, whereas no such concern was identified in the 2026 responses. None of the 528 responses contained an explicit recommendation considered likely to cause immediate or serious patient harm. Conclusions Performance changed in a model-specific rather than uniformly progressive manner. The findings represent sampled first-pass responses to clearly formulated guideline-derived questions rather than stable estimates of model performance or reproducibility. LLMs may support access to male infertility information, but verification against authoritative sources and appropriate human oversight remain necessary.

items.title: Explainable artificial intelligence reveals spatially divergent effects of global change on mammals
items.abstract: Abstract Understanding how global change reshapes species distributions remains a central challenge in ecology, yet most global assessments treat environmental drivers as static, uniform, or aggregate influences. This obscures where, why, and how specific drivers generate ecological risk or opportunity. Here, we apply explainable machine learning to assess how climate averages, variability, extremes, and land cover are projected to reshape future distributions of 1,992 terrestrial mammals. Using Shapley Additive Explanations with species distribution models, we quantify the directional contribution of 16 environmental drivers and track how these contributions change over space and time. We propose two ecological diagnostics, directional turnovers and favorability shifts, that reveal where drivers switch from favorable to unfavorable, or the reverse, and where their influence strengthens or weakens without sign reversal. While not designed to infer causation, our framework assesses whether projected spatial patterns align with ecological expectations. We show that climate extremes impose intense but spatially restricted impacts, temperature-related drivers dominate exposure patterns, particularly for specialist species, and the same driver can impose risk in one region while creating opportunity in another. By decomposing projected biodiversity change into driver-specific signatures, our framework advances biodiversity forecasting toward a more actionable understanding of ecological risk and opportunity.

items.title: EXPLORING CHATGPT’S ROLE AS AN AUTOMATED WRITING EVALUATION TOOL: A STUDY IN VIETNAMESE HIGH SCHOOL EFL CLASSROOMS
items.abstract: Since its launch, ChatGPT has become a widely used tool by students for classroom exercises and home assignments. This study examines the role of ChatGPT as an automatic writing evaluation (AWE) tool in assisting Vietnamese high school students in self-correcting grammar and vocabulary errors in their descriptive writing assignments. The participants were five 18-year-old students at a private high school in Ho Chi Minh City. Before utilizing ChatGPT to revise original drafts, the participants were tasked with writing seven assignments based on Cambridge English Key (KET) exam picture prompts. Data collection included pre- and post-ChatGPT-usage writing assessments, screenshots of revisions, and some questionnaires exploring feedback engagement and reasoning behind acceptance or rejection of ChatGPT’s suggestions. Results showed improved writing, highlighting ChatGPT’s strengths in correcting grammar and enhancing vocabulary. Students engaged deeply with feedback, selectively accepting or rejecting suggestions based on their writing context and demonstrating enhanced self-assessment and learning independence. This autonomy is noteworthy and valuable in large classrooms where teacher feedback is limited. However, the participants expressed mixed levels of trust in the tool, especially when the suggestions seemed unclear or incompatible with their writing style, and often sought teacher validation. While ChatGPT promotes autonomous learning, it should complement, not replace, teacher feedback.

items.title: Exploring collaborative problem-solving in AI-assisted robotics education
items.abstract: Prompt engineering (PE) involves creating, improving, and deploying prompts to improve large language model (LLM) performance. Despite its increasing importance, many students lack skills in this area. Although frameworks for prompt design and process exist, theory-based instructional tools for improving prompt engineering skills are uncommon for developing collaborative problem-solving (CPS) skills in Robotics Education. This study adopted a PE strategy in AI-assisted robotics education, particularly for developing CPS. PE has four scaffolding stages: Alignment, Adaptation, Autonomy, and Innovation, and was analysed through four PE codes: Alignment Specification, Adaptive Refinement, Auditing, and Innovation. This study adopted a non-randomised, multi-site, criterion-group comparative design, with 243 undergraduate students categorised according to their ability group. This study used epistemic network analysis (ENA) to identify the co-occurrences of PE and CPS skills and examine the differences in conversation patterns among ability groups. The findings revealed distinct PE–CPS discourse configurations across ability groups. These results underscore the pedagogical value of scaffolding in developing PE skills and fostering students’ productivity in a synergetic learning environment.

items.title: Exploring foreign language learners' GenAI-coexisted peer argumentation
items.abstract: Argumentation has been widely used as a discussion activity in the English as a foreign language (EFL) classroom. Nevertheless, peer argumentation combined with generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) remains limited despite increasing recognition of GenAI usage among EFL learners. To address this gap, we adopted the pragmatic-dialectic approach to argumentation and the proposition of intersubjectivity, and explored the argumentation process of six Chinese undergraduate students in their English newspaper reading course. A qualitative case study was used to analyze transcripts of peer argumentation, responses to an open-ended questionnaire and screenshots of chats with GenAI. Findings showed that students' peer argumentation was at a dynamic continuum, shifting from GenAI-dominated pseudo-argumentation with lowly dialogic moves to GenAI-coexisted authentic argumentation with highly dialogic moves. The study also yielded explanations for the changes, which involved the reciprocal awareness of human and/or GenAI, the outcome and the process of constructing a shared new understanding among heterogeneous interlocutors. The findings provided insights for the educational significance of the argumentative activities centered on the intersubjectivity in GenAI-coexisted language learning settings.

items.title: Exploring GenAI Chatbot Use for L2 Learning: A Mixed-Methods Study of Foundation-Year Students in Oman
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots have increasingly become part of many university students' English as a second language (L2) learning. However, little is known about how students in general foundation programmes use them during the move from Arabic-medium schooling to English-medium higher education. This sequential explanatory mixed-methods study examined GenAI chatbot use among foundation-year students at a private university in Oman. A questionnaire (N = 262) covered usage patterns, perceived usefulness for L2 skills, AI output verification practices, challenges and support needs, and was followed by two focus groups (n = 15). Results showed that ChatGPT was the dominant tool (91.2%) that students accessed mainly by smartphone (80.5%). The most common frequency was "sometimes" (47.3%), while 42.4% of respondents reported using chatbots "always" or "often". Most students (57.6%) switched between English and Arabic while interacting with GenAI chatbots. Students rated chatbots as clearly useful for writing, speaking and reading, but not for listening. They also valued grammar and vocabulary corrections by chatbots more than their feedback on writing or speaking assignments. More than two-thirds of respondents preferred teacher feedback on their writing (72.9%). The most frequently reported challenges were incorrect information (43.5%) and unclear responses (35.1%), while the most common verification strategy of generated content was asking a teacher (46.2%). Focus-group participants described purpose-driven but largely unplanned prompting, translation-mediated comprehension, concern about overreliance, inconsistent teacher stances, and a need for classroom-embedded guidance. Chatbot use for L2 learning among foundation-year students can be interpreted as a tool-mediated activity largely outside formal L2 instructional design, with teachers as epistemic anchors. The study recommends early, skill-specific, teacher-mediated AI literacy instruction in foundation programmes.

items.abstract: This article examines the role of rural extension in scaling up agroecology in Brazil, arguing that such a transition depends on institutional mediations capable of linking knowledge, public policies, and territorial practices. By revisiting the principles of agroecological rural extension and analyzing their institutionalization within the National Policy for Technical Assistance and Rural Extension (PNATER), the study shows a progressive dilution of these principles throughout policy implementation. At the same time, it highlights the limited academic engagement with the interface between agroecology and rural extension. Based on this diagnosis, the article proposes a strategic agenda to strengthen agroecological rural extension, structured around four axes: progressive reframing of PNATER, valorization of sociotechnical arrangements, strengthening of training processes, and consolidation of a dedicated research agenda.

items.title: Factors Associated with Disability Level Among Adult Patients with Low Back Pain
items.abstract: Background: Low back pain can restrict functioning through interacting symptoms, beliefs, and contextual demands. Qualitative inquiry can clarify how these influences are experienced. Objective: To explore perceived influences on disability and how they interact to restrict or support everyday functioning among adults with persistent low back pain. Methods: An interpretive qualitative study used purposive maximum-variation sampling to include 18 adults aged 25–66 years. Individual semi-structured interviews explored symptoms, movement, sleep, work, family roles, healthcare, and self-management. Oswestry Disability Index scores informed lower-, moderate-, and higher-disability sampling profiles. Interview material underwent reflexive thematic analysis, including examination of contrasting accounts and author review of interpretations. Results: Participants comprised 10 women and eight men; five had lower, seven moderate, and six higher disability profiles. Five themes were developed: Living with Unpredictable Pain; Fear, Threat, and Shrinking Activity; Caught Between Recovery and Livelihood; Support, Dependence, and Identity; and Clinical Explanations, Confidence, and Control. Accounts connected restrictions with anticipated flares, perceived damage, poor sleep, work and financial pressures, and changing family roles. Contrasting accounts described participation alongside pain when movement felt manageable and support preserved involvement. Conclusion: Disability was experienced within the interaction of symptoms, interpretations, relationships, and practical circumstances. Assessment and rehabilitation should consider barriers to meaningful participation alongside pain. Keywords: low back pain; disability; qualitative research; biopsychosocial factors; fear avoidance; self-efficacy; occupational health.

items.title: Factors associated with generative AI chatbot acceptance among medical students with prior academic use: a cross-sectional study based on an extended technology acceptance model
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots are becoming increasingly embedded in medical education, providing students with on-demand support for learning, clinical reasoning, and academic tasks. However, the psychological and technological factors that shape medical students’ acceptance of these tools remain insufficiently understood. This study examined acceptance among medical students with prior academic use of GenAI chatbots by extending the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to include AI literacy (AIL) and perceived security and privacy (PSP), and by examining their associations with perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), attitude toward using GenAI (ATG), and behavioral intention to use GenAI (BIG). A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among medical students at Hormozgan University of Medical Sciences (HUMS), Iran, between May and June 2026. Eligibility required prior academic use of a GenAI chatbot. Data were collected using a structured, self-administered questionnaire and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The measurement model was assessed for reliability and validity, while the structural model was evaluated using path coefficients (β), coefficients of determination ( R ²), and effect sizes ( f ²). Of the 292 students invited, 267 completed the survey, and 252 participants with prior academic use of GenAI chatbots were included in the final analysis (mean age, 22.64 ± 2.28 years; 147 [58.3%] female). The measurement model demonstrated adequate reliability and validity. AIL was positively associated with PEOU (β = 0.479, p < 0.001), while PSP was positively associated with PU (β = 0.157, p = 0.005). PEOU and PU were positively associated with ATG, and ATG showed the strongest association with BIG (β = 0.524, p < 0.001). The model explained 38.7% of the variance in BIG, with R ² values ranging from 0.229 to 0.387 across the endogenous constructs. The findings indicate that medical students’ acceptance of GenAI chatbots is associated with AIL and PSP alongside the core TAM constructs of PEOU and PU, with ATG showing the strongest association with BIG. Strengthening AIL and establishing clear privacy and security policies may support the informed and responsible integration of GenAI chatbots into medical education.

items.title: Feature Engineering for Biological Sequence and Protein Structure Prediction
items.abstract: Feature engineering remains central to predictive modeling in computational biology, governing how DNA, RNAand protein sequences are converted into numerical forms amenable to machine learning. The field hasprogressed from compact composition based descriptors such as amino acid composition (AAC) and dipeptidecomposition (DPC) to correlation based representations (pseudo amino acid composition, PseAAC, pseudoK-tuple nucleotide composition, PseKNC), evolutionary profiles (position specific scoring matrices, PSSM), and,more recently, to deep representation learning and biological foundation models. This narrative review focuseson biological sequence prediction, with particular emphasis on proteins and structure derived features. Webegin with Chou's five step framework for predictor construction, benchmark curation and redundancyreduction using CD-HIT and MMseqs2, and the specific challenges of multi label and hierarchical prediction. Wethen survey handcrafted descriptors, feature selection and dimensionality reduction, and the adaptation ofnatural language processing methods to biological sequences, including k-mer embeddings, convolutional andrecurrent architectures, and protein and genomic foundation models, including Transformer models such asESM-2 and DNABERT-2, the ESMFold structure predictor, and Hyena based genomic models. We distinguishthree common adaptation strategies: frozen embedding extraction, full fine tuning and parameter efficient finetuning (PEFT) - and discuss hybrid fusion of handcrafted and learned features, structure founded encodings(DSSP, Foldseek 3Di, ProstT5, SES-Adapter), and the role of explainable AI (SHAP, LIME, Integrated Gradients).Throughout we emphasize homology evaluation, nested validation to avoid selection leakage, confidencebased use of predicted structures, and cautious interpretation of attribution. We close with practical guidelinesfor choosing a representation under different data and compute regimes and outline open challenges.

items.title: Fiqh Education in the Context of Artificial intelligence: Shifts in Pedagogy, Authority, and Religious Literacy
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded the use of information and learning resources in Islamic Religious Education, including Fiqh learning, while raising concerns regarding pedagogy, the authority and validity of religious knowledge, and students’ ability to evaluate AI-generated information. This study examines the use of AI in Islamic education and synthesizes its implications for Fiqh learning, focusing on pedagogy, the authority and validity of religious knowledge, and religious literacy and AI literacy. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted on 25 scholarly articles published between 2020 and 2026 and retrieved from Scopus, Google Scholar, and the Indonesian scholarly databases GARUDA/SINTA. Searches used combinations of keywords related to artificial intelligence, generative AI, ChatGPT, Islamic education, Islamic religious education, and fiqh education. Articles were selected based on their relevance to Islamic education or Fiqh learning and to the analytical dimensions of the study. Data were analyzed through coding, thematic categorization, cross-source comparison, and thematic synthesis. The findings indicate that AI is increasingly used to support personalized learning, information exploration, learning-material development, and instructional interaction. However, its use also intensifies the need for source verification, information validation, and teacher guidance. The synthesis further highlights the importance of integrating religious literacy and AI literacy to enable students to evaluate AI-generated information critically and responsibly. Based on these findings, the study proposes an AI-assisted but teacher-guided Fiqh learning framework that positions AI as a learning support tool, teachers as pedagogical and knowledge mediators, and students as active evaluators of information.

items.title: Foundation Models for Autonomous Space Robotics: Architectures, Physical Adaptation, and Validation
items.abstract: Space robots must interpret tasks and act despite unfamiliar dynamics, difficult sensing conditions, and limited opportunities for human intervention. Foundation models offer reusable perceptual and behavioral knowledge, but their value depends on how that knowledge reaches physical execution. This critical review follows space-specific requirements through perception, prediction, planning, and action to deployment and validation, emphasizing orbital manipulation and proximity operations. Terrestrial comparisons establish benefits of particular pretraining stages and model interfaces; their transfer to space dynamics and constrained onboard operation remains insufficiently tested. Event cameras offer timely motion observations across strong illumination contrasts, while spiking neural networks provide possible routes to sparse local computation. We examine how sensor degradation, state estimation and computing choices affect feedback and recovery. Higher action throughput need not yield fresher feedback; lower processor power can also coexist with higher energy per inference. We organize validation as an iterative sim-to-ground-to-space pathway, connecting physical tests with telemetry-based diagnosis and closed-loop revalidation. A satellite-capture example links observations to approach, contact and recovery, while a corresponding protocol separates generalization from adaptation with limited target-domain interaction. These comparisons identify what models already contribute and the physical evidence needed to support autonomous space operation.

items.title: Foundation-Model Supervision of Distilled Potentials for Million-Atom Molecular Dynamics
items.abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials distilled from foundation models enable fast large-scale molecular dynamics (MD), but they can fail locally in chemical environments that their training data did not sample. System-averaged error metrics and small random audits often miss such sparse or isolated failures. Here we use an exact equivariant foundation model, MACE-MPA-0, to check every atom of million-atom production simulations. Reorganizing two-layer MACE inference into a receiver-chunked three-pass schedule that keeps no per-edge intermediates resident reduces the marginal memory per atom 340-fold, evaluates up to $2.86\times10^{7}$ atoms on a single H200 GPU, and supervises $10^{6}$-atom trajectories in LAMMPS at 1.3% of the run time. Distilled MACE students run four to nine times slower than NEP89 with 0.95-1.28 times the teacher's force error against density functional theory (DFT). In molten SiO$_2$, whole-system checks uncover a persistent tail of under-coordinated atoms hidden by the system-averaged error and an isolated, unphysical O-O contact that a 1% random audit misses 94% of the time. On-the-fly retraining on teacher-labelled 13-Å clusters, with the force loss restricted to their inner 6 Å, removes three quarters of the failure tail and the kilobar-level pressure biases in SiO$_2$ and compressed water; the repair converges to the teacher, not to DFT.

items.title: From Anthropomorphism to Trust: Unpacking the Role of Authenticity in Generative AI and Large Language Models—A Structured Literature Review and Future Research Agenda
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has changed the conditions under which users encounter and evaluate machine-produced communication. In systems based on large language models, conversational output is no longer merely functional; it can be fluent, context-aware, and socially legible, inviting judgments that extend beyond usefulness, accuracy, or efficiency. Yet the literature still tends to treat anthropomorphism, perceived authenticity, and trust as largely separate constructs, without sufficiently explaining how human-like cues become credible in the eyes of users and how this credibility shapes trust. To address this problem, the present structured literature review synthesizes recent research on anthropomorphism, authenticity-related evaluations, and trust in AI-mediated interaction, with particular attention to conversational AI, generative AI, and LLM-based systems. A structured search in the Web of Science Core Collection identified 655 records; after duplicate removal, screening, and eligibility assessment, 96 studies were retained for qualitative synthesis. The analysis identifies several interrelated thematic patterns, including anthropomorphic cues and social presence, authenticity-related mechanisms in AI-mediated communication, trust formation and calibration, boundary conditions, and behavioral responses to conversational AI. On this basis, the review develops an integrative conceptual framework and proposes perceived anthropomorphic authenticity as a review-derived construct for examining how users evaluate human-like AI communication in relation to trust. The study contributes to human–AI interaction research by clarifying the role of authenticity-related evaluations between anthropomorphic cues and calibrated trust and by identifying conditions under which human-like communication may be associated with trust, skepticism, overreliance, or trust erosion.

items.title: From Assistance to Dependence: Investigating the Effects of Generative AI on Student Learning, Retention, and Study Effort
items.abstract: Purpose: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), including tools such as ChatGPT, is increasingly used by university students for explanations, summaries, problem-solving, feedback, and academic support. This paper examines whether such assistance supports learning or may encourage dependence that affects long-term retention and independent thinking. Methods: The study uses secondary research and a descriptive synthesis of published experimental studies, randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses. No primary data were collected and no new statistical meta-analysis was conducted. Results: The reviewed studies generally report positive effects on academic performance and engagement. Reported effect sizes include approximately g = 0.712 across 69 experimental studies, Hedges’ g = 0.577 across 37 studies, and an effect size of approximately 0.804 across 57 studies. However, one randomized controlled study reported 45-day retention of 57.5% for a ChatGPT-assisted group compared with 68.5% for a traditional-learning group. Conclusion: GenAI can be a useful learning assistant when students actively use it for explanation, feedback, comparison, and clarification. However, completing tasks efficiently should not be treated as proof of deep or lasting learning. Students should retain opportunities for independent recall, reasoning, analysis, and problem-solving.

items.title: From Chronology to Physiology: A Critical Translational Assessment of Artificial Intelligence for Precision Healthspan Measurement
items.abstract: Healthspan, the period of life free from major chronic disease and disability, is a central geroscience outcome, yet its prediction remains difficult due to its multidimensional and heterogeneous nature. In this review, we synthesize advances in artificial intelligence (AI) for precision healthspan assessment, shifting from chronological age estimates toward physiologically grounded, individualized health trajectory forecasting. We examine supervised, deep, self-supervised, and reinforcement learning approaches, alongside AI-based biomarkers of aging, including epigenetic, proteomic, imaging, and wearable-derived digital biomarkers. We also discuss multimodal AI integrating multi-omic, imaging, and sensor data, explainable AI for clinical translation, and key issues in validation, regulation, ethics, bias, privacy, and equitable access. We critically appraise the level of validation supporting each major technology, distinguish biological-age estimation from true healthspan prediction, and separate predictive performance from demonstrated clinical utility. In this review, we conclude that AI-powered healthspan algorithms hold promise for shifting healthcare from reactive disease management to proactive, personalized aging management, but current evidence remains strongest for prediction and weakest for clinical utility; translation will require rigorous external and prospective validation, standardized outcomes, robust ethical and regulatory frameworks, and equitable implementation.

items.title: From curated datasets to social-media reality: In-the-wild, multimodal, and generalizable deepfake detection
items.abstract: Deepfake detection has advanced rapidly alongside progress in generative adversarial networks, diffusion models, neural rendering, and multimodal synthesis. However, strong performance on curated benchmark datasets does not necessarily translate into reliable performance in real-world environments, where manipulated media are affected by platform compression, reposting, post-processing, multimodal inconsistency, temporal drift, and evolving generation pipelines. This review examines deepfake detection from the perspective of in-the-wild robustness, multimodal reasoning, and cross-domain generalization. It first clarifies the conceptual foundations of in-the-wild and generalizable deepfake detection, then reviews the data ecosystem, including benchmark datasets, real-world media conditions, multimodal data gaps, annotation quality, and benchmark aging. The review further analyzes the major causes of detector failure under realistic deployment conditions, including generator shift, platform-induced degradation, modality mismatch, language and speaker variation, and broader contextual diversity. It then compares major methodological families, including artifact-based methods, deep representation-based approaches, transfer-based learning, domain adaptation, domain generalization, and multimodal detection strategies, with emphasis on their relevance to real-world robustness. Finally, the review discusses evaluation practices, external validation, realistic benchmarking, and future directions such as continually updated benchmarks, missing-modality-robust systems, uncertainty-aware detection, provenance integration, and foundation-model-based approaches. Overall, the review argues that reliable deepfake detection requires a shift from benchmark-centered optimization toward robust, multimodal, and deployment-oriented evaluation and design.

items.title: From Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment to Human Rights Auditing
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in high-impact domains has heightened concerns regarding the protection of fundamental rights. While the EU AI Act introduces the Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) as a key governance mechanism for certain high-risk AI systems, its broader conceptual role remains underexplored. This chapter argues that the FRIA should not be understood merely as a compliance obligation but as an emerging form of human rights auditing for algorithmic systems. Drawing on audit theory, human rights due diligence, and algorithmic accountability scholarship, it develops a conceptual framework that reframes the FRIA as a rights-based assurance mechanism. It further proposes a Rights Safeguards Audit Ladder to assess the maturity of organizational safeguards and illustrates its application through AI-based credit scoring. We contribute to AI governance debates by showing how human rights auditing can bridge the gap between regulatory compliance, organizational accountability, and continuous rights protection in high-risk AI systems.

items.title: From GAN-Based Models to GPT-5: A Taxonomy-Guided Study of Human Performance in Detecting Deepfake Face Images
items.abstract: Generative models for deepfakes have rapidly evolved from GAN-based architectures to diffusion models and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, empirical research on human performance in detecting deepfake face images has not kept pace. It remains unclear if (and how) detection performance varies across generative models and whether model-specific training improves detection more effectively than general-purpose training. In this paper, we propose the \emph{Deepfake Face Artifact Taxonomy} (DFAT), a cross-model taxonomy of human-recognizable visual artifacts in deepfake face images, based on which we build both general-purpose and model-specific training materials. Through an online experiment ($n = 524$), we examined human performance in detecting deepfake face images and evaluated training efficacy across five representative generative models: three GAN-based, one diffusion-based, and one MLLM (GPT-5). Our results show that participants' detection accuracy was strongly model-dependent and that images generated by more recent and advanced models were not necessarily harder to detect. After training, participants achieved significant performance gains across most conditions, and their improvement varied by model. Notably, model-specific training generally yielded greater numerical gains than general-purpose training. In a five-month follow-up test ($n = 342$), we observed no significant decline in detection accuracy and no significant increase in perceived stress. Overall, our findings provide actionable insights for designing effective, sustainable, and targeted training programs to counter the growing threat posed by deepfakes.

items.title: From HPV infection to cervical precancer: Molecular mechanisms, immune microenvironment and emerging technologies
items.abstract: Cervical cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women globally, with persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection as the primary etiological factor. Cervical precancerous lesions, including high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions and adenocarcinoma in situ, represent the critical window for intervention prior to invasive cancer development. However, additional factors such as immunosuppression, smoking, and microbiome composition also play crucial roles in the development of cervical precancerous lesions. While HPV vaccination, screening, and treatment have reduced cancer incidence, these must be complemented by personalized approaches that target the molecular mechanisms driving carcinogenesis. Key dysregulated tumor suppressors (e.g., p16) and signaling pathways (PI3K/AKT/mTOR, Wnt/β-catenin) highlight the need for advanced therapeutic strategies. The immune microenvironment also plays a critical role in cancer progression, suggesting potential for immunotherapy. Promising biomarkers like p16, Ki67, and microRNAs require integration with technologies such as single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics for deeper insights into tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment dynamics. Additionally, while deep learning models hold promise in improving diagnostic accuracy for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), challenges such as data variability and interpretability need addressing. In conclusion, incorporating genomics, transcriptomics, immunotherapy, and artificial intelligence will enable more personalized and effective interventions, ultimately reducing the global burden of cervical cancer.

items.title: From Indenture to Electronics: Brokered Labor Regimes in Johor, Malaysia
items.abstract: Abstract This article develops the concept of a brokered dormitory labor regime (BDLR) to analyze Johor, Malaysia’s electrical and electronics export-processing zones, where debt-financed recruitment, deceptive contracting, and restricted mobility synchronize labor turnover with the accelerating demand for semiconductor manufacturing driven by artificial intelligence. Two intermediaries, the labor agent and the kadar, secure this synchronization by controlling workers’ social reproduction. Tracing this regime’s genealogy to the nineteenth-century kangani and kangchu systems in the Straits Settlements, the article argues that the BDLR reactivates a colonial infrastructure of coerced migrant labor, revealing a recurring pattern of asynchronous synchronization between capital and labor across successive industrial revolutions.

items.title: From knowledge retrieval to generation: a comprehensive study of RAG's architectures, evolution, and applications
items.abstract: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in natural language understanding, generation, and reasoning, but their reliance on static parametric knowledge still leads to knowledge staleness, hallucinations, limited domain adaptability, weak traceability, and high updating costs in knowledge-intensive scenarios. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) helps address these limitations by incorporating external knowledge sources into the generation process, making it an important approach for improving factual grounding, knowledge timeliness, and evidence traceability. However, existing RAG research is increasingly fragmented across architectures, retrieval and generation strategies, evaluation methods, application scenarios, deployment constraints, and security risks. To provide a systematic understanding of this field, this survey reviews RAG research through a structured and transparent review protocol. We organize the review around three major dimensions: the system stack and paradigm evolution of RAG, evaluation methods and application evidence, and practical deployment and security challenges. Specifically, we analyze the core components of RAG systems, synthesize their evolution from Naive RAG to Agentic RAG, examine evaluation metrics and stress-testing protocols, summarize benchmark datasets and domain applications, and discuss deployment constraints and emerging risks such as prompt injection, data poisoning, retrieval hijacking, privacy leakage, and citation laundering. This survey provides a taxonomy-oriented, evaluation-aware, and deployment-conscious reference for understanding the development, limitations, and future directions of RAG systems.

items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents can read sensitive information, execute privileged commands, and move data betweenenterprise systems. Existing authentication and authorization checks remain necessary, but a tool call can be permittedwhile the sequence of calls produces a result outside the authorized business task. This paper addresses a practicalsecurity problem: how can an enterprise detect and stop a harmful sequence of individually permitted actions beforea damaging action executes? It proposes Trajectory-Aware Zero Trust (TA-ZT), a vendor-neutral referencearchitecture that combines DoD Zero Trust pillars, CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model v2, task-scoped authorization,action history, data lineage, and independent policy enforcement. The proposed architecture allows a security gatewayto approve, pause, or deny a sensitive action using both its immediate parameters and its task-level context. The paperexplains the security gap, expected organizational value, control mapping, engineering components, exampleworkflow, test methodology, and phased implementation. It is a conceptual research proposal, not a deployed orexperimentally validated system. items.title: From Physique Concerns to Pan-Appearance Anxiety in the Digital Age:A Dual-Database Bibliometric Analysis of Health-Related Research (2006–2026)
items.abstract: 1. Background In recent years, the escalating global burden of appearance-related distress has transformed social physique anxiety into a multidimensional public health challenge. Although the rapid expansion of digital environments significantly exacerbates appearance vulnerabilities and the volume of academic literature has grown substantially, a comprehensive quantitative mapping of the field's evolutionary trajectory remains lacking. Previous reviews were often limited to a single database, which may result in a biased representation of global trends and fail to capture the core theoretical transition from specific "physique anxiety" (focusing strictly on adiposity and muscularity) to broader "social appearance anxiety" (encompassing global aesthetic evaluations like facial features and skin tone). 2. Objective This project aims to systematically visualize the knowledge structure, spatiotemporal distribution, and developmental trends of social physique anxiety research by integrating literature from the past two decades (January 1, 2006, to August 15, 2026). Specific objectives include: Mapping and evaluating the global collaboration networks among authors, institutions, and countries. Identifying current research hotspots through keyword co-occurrence and structural clustering analyses. Building a dynamic predictive framework via keyword burst detection to forecast emerging frontiers that will shape future targeted behavioral interventions and clinical practice. 3. Methods Summary This study employs bibliometric methods to systematically retrieve and integrate data from two major authoritative databases: Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and Scopus. After excluding ineligible data, the records are rigorously cleaned using a Python-based triple-verification deduplication algorithm (BibexPy framework), resulting in a final dataset of 624 unique eligible articles. The harmonized data is then subjected to in-depth network mapping and visualization analysis using CiteSpace and VOSviewer. 4. Expected Results & ImplicationsThis project aims to comprehensively elucidate the structural shifts within this domain over the past two decades, with expected key findings including:Global Contributions and Networks: Highlighting the leadership of countries like Turkey, the United States, and Canada in driving international contributions, and revealing how transnational collaboration networks among highly productive academic institutions advance theoretical progress. Thematic Evolution Trajectories: Delineating the shift in research focus from early instrument development (e.g., psychometric validations) to a contemporary strategic focus on transdiagnostic psychopathology and holistic well-being (quality of life) interventions. Impact of Digital Culture: Highlighting the exacerbating role of modern "digital filter culture" and social media addiction in amplifying appearance-related distress and broader social anxiety among youth. Frontier Interventions: Predicting and emphasizing the emerging potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven personalized psychological interventions, digital phenotyping, and exposure therapies in proactive mental health management. In summary, by delineating established domains such as eating disorder comorbidity and tracking emerging trajectories in digital health, this research provides a vital evidence-based framework for optimizing targeted behavioral interventions. It also emphasizes the core value of protective mechanisms like self-compassion in mitigating negative self-evaluation and promoting exercise adherence.

items.title: From Prefabricated Content to Situated Generation: A Four-Wave Longitudinal Study of AI-Mediated Museum Surfaces and Spaces
items.abstract: Generative AI changes a basic condition of interactive surfaces and spaces (ISS): visitor-facing content can be produced during interaction rather than fully authored before it. We report a longitudinal qualitative study with 23 Chinese science museum practitioners, interviewed annually from 2023 to 2026 (retention 23 to 19) and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Participants' accounts moved from anticipated epistemic and operational risks, through backstage experimentation and visitor-facing trials, toward situated governance and renewed questions about the purpose of museum interaction. Following these changes over time shows how generative AI reconfigured the design problems of museum ISS: generated content appeared under institutional authority; inference delay became publicly and bodily experienced; concurrent touch, gesture, and speech created ambiguous multi-user intent; and post-generation editing could leave curators selecting within an AI-defined possibility space. We conceptualize the resulting shift as a movement from prefabricated display to situated generation and formulate four design propositions concerning provenance at the point of display, spatially appropriate fallback, multi-intent negotiation, and curatorial control before generation. These propositions are grounded in practitioner accounts rather than evaluations of implemented solutions.

items.title: From Rules to Autonomous Agents: The Evolution of Artificial Intelligence, Human-AI Integration, and the Governance of Agentic Systems-A Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has evolved from rule-based symbolic systems into learning architectures capable of perception, prediction, content generation, reasoning, planning, tool use, and increasingly autonomous action. This qualitative literature review examines this transition as more than a technological chronology. It interprets AI evolution through five interrelated dimensions: technological evolution, capability expansion, changing human roles, human–AI integration, and governance. Drawing on contemporary peer-reviewed literature published primarily between 2020 and 2026, the review identifies seven thematic developments. AI has progressed from encoded rules toward learned representations and goal-directed action; generative AI has expanded AI into a general-purpose content collaborator; agentic AI adds planning, memory, tool use, and iterative task execution; human roles increasingly shift from operator toward collaborator, delegator, and governor; human–AI complementarity remains conditional rather than automatic; effective deployment requires calibrated rather than maximal trust; and governance requirements increase as AI systems acquire greater operational agency. The article proposes the Evolution–Capability–Role–Integration–Governance (ECRIG) framework to explain these relationships. The framework suggests that sustainable benefits from advanced AI emerge when technological capability, human role allocation, interaction architecture, and governance mechanisms develop jointly. The review concludes that the central challenge of the agentic-AI era is not choosing between humans and machines, but designing accountable systems in which increasingly capable artificial agents remain aligned with meaningful human goals, authority, and oversight.

items.title: From workplace learning to professional identity formation: Examining the mediating role of belonging in medical students
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Professional identity formation (PIF) is increasingly understood as a socially situated workplace learning process through which medical students develop identities and practices of physicians. Through participation in clinical work within the clinical learning environment (CLE), students learn what it means to become members of the profession. Within this context, a sense of belonging may be an important mechanism linking the CLE to PIF. However, quantitative evidence examining these relationships remains limited. This study examined whether sense of belonging mediates the relationship between the CLE and PIF. METHODS: This cross-sectional study used data from 459 undergraduate clinical students in Indonesia collected between November 1 and December 15, 2024. Students completed three validated instruments: the Professional Identity Formation (PIF) questionnaire, the Undergraduate Clinical Education Environment Measure (UCEEM), and the Belongingness Scale-Clinical Placement Experience (BES-CPE). Structural equation modelling (SEM) was employed to assess whether sense of belonging functioned as a mediator between the CLE and PIF. RESULTS: < 0.001). The SEM mediation model demonstrated good fit (SRMR = 0.038, CFI = 0.96, TLI = 0.94), indicating that belonging partially mediated the relationship between the CLE and PIF. DISCUSSION: The findings reveal that PIF are positively linked to both CLE and a sense of belonging. In addition, sense of belonging functions as a significant statistical mediator in the pathway linking the CLE to PIF. These findings suggest that workplace learning experiences contribute to PIF not only directly but also through fostering students' sense of belonging. Creating supportive clinical environments that promote participation, inclusion, and membership may therefore strengthen medical students' PIF.

items.title: Fundamental Rights in the Digital Era: Reinterpreting Liberty, Privacy and Dignity
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technologies has fundamentally altered the manner in which individuals communicate, access information, participate in public life, conduct economic activities, and exercise personal autonomy. The transition from an analogue to a digitally mediated society has consequently transformed the environment in which fundamental rights operate. In India, constitutional guarantees contained in Part III of the Constitution were originally formulated in an era preceding the internet, social media, artificial intelligence, biometric identification, algorithmic decision-making and large-scale data processing. Nevertheless, the constitutional framework has demonstrated considerable capacity to respond to technological change through judicial interpretation, particularly by expanding the meaning of liberty, privacy and dignity under Article 21 of Constitution of India. The Apex Court of India has played an important role in this constitutional transformation. Land mark judgments such as Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India, Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India and K.S. Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) v. Union of India have contributed to the development of a fundamental rights-based understanding of digital governance and technological freedom. At the same time, the emergence of artificial intelligence, facial recognition, pervasive surveillance, data profiling, deepfakes, online harassment, misinformation and platform-based censorship presents challenges that cannot always be addressed through traditional interpretations of constitutional rights. This paper examines how fundamental rights and human rights must be understood in the digital era, with particular emphasis on Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution of India. As these three articles are golden triangle, stated under Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India case. It argues that digital constitutionalism requires the protection of not merely physical freedom but also informational autonomy, decisional freedom, digital expression, anonymity, personal identity and human dignity. The paper further examines the relationship between privacy and national security, freedom of speech and online regulation, and technological innovation and constitutional accountability. It concludes that technological advancement must remain compatible with constitutional morality, proportionality, transparency, accountability and the dignity of the individual.

items.title: Gamified digital training tools for enhancing indirect vision skills in preclinical dental education: a randomized control trial
items.abstract: Abstract Background Preclinical dental training emphasizes indirect vision using mirrors for precision and ergonomics to prevent musculoskeletal disorders. Students often face challenges with suboptimal posture and extended procedure times. Digital gamified tools like mobile app and ImageJ software enable objective and repeatable assessments, although targeted studies on indirect vision improvement remain limited. This randomized controlled trial evaluated the effectiveness of digital training in improving precision of performance and ergonomic posture during indirect vision tasks. Aim To assess the impact of gamified smartphone training on indirect vision skills in preclinical BDS students. Methods The aim of this study was to assess the impact of gamified smartphone training on indirect vision skills in preclinical BDS students. Parallel RCT at Manipal College of Dental Sciences, Mangalore ( n = 68 s-year BDS; control n = 34, intervention n = 34). Intervention group: Total 40 min, with each session 20-min with break Pac-Man 256 indirect mirror training on personal device. Both: Standardized phantom head cavity outline coloring. Outcomes: ImageJ % error (v1.54p), time (min), and modified CADEP score.Shapiro-Wilk test for normality and Mann-Whitney U test for group comparisons. Results 87.5% (14/16) of the variables were non-normal ( p < 0.05) in both groups. The training group showed reduced time, lower error, and superior CADEP scores compared to the controls ( p < 0.05). Conclusion Brief gamified digital training significantly improves indirect vision, efficiency, and ergonomics of dental students. Overall, gamified cellular device-based indirect vision training improved the accuracy of cavity preparation. We recommend low-cost integration into undergraduate curricula. Trial registration The study was Retrospectively registered with the Clinical Trials Registry - India (CTRI), CTRI Reg. Date 27/07/2026 with registration number CTRI/2026/07/114,792.

items.title: Generative AI and Digital Inequality in South African Higher Education: Students’ Experiences of Access and Meaningful Use at a Rural University
items.abstract: This study examined the conditions that enable or constrain undergraduate students’ access to, and meaningful use of, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) at a rural South African university. Using an interpretivist qualitative case study design, researchers conducted semi-structured, face-to-face interviews with 12 undergraduate students with prior experience using GenAI for academic purposes. Data were analysed thematically following Braun and Clarke’s ix-phase approach. Four interconnected conditions shaped students’ experiences: device and connectivity reliability, the affordability of sustained data access, artificial intelligence (AI) literacy, and institutional infrastructure and training. Students consistently perceived GenAI as useful, but their capacity to realise that usefulness depended on resources and competencies that were unevenly distributed. The study uses this gap to extend TAM’s construct of perceived usefulness with a distinct construct of realised usefulness, and this study argues that generative AI introduces a literacy demand, critical evaluation of machine-generated, plausible-sounding but sometimes inaccurate output. The study contributes to digital-inequality scholarship by extending the access–skills–benefits distinction into the generative AI context and by identifying the gap between perceived and realised usefulness as a mechanism through which existing inequalities may be reproduced. The study recommends that institutional responses combine connectivity, affordable access, structured AI literacy instruction, and explicit academic guidance, rather than treating any one of these as sufficient on its own.

items.title: Generative AI as a cognitive partner: personalised GPTs and differentiated learning in undergraduate teacher education
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly framed as a catalyst for deeper learning rather than simple automation. This design-based study investigated how personalised GPT agents were used as cognitive partners by pre-service teachers in an undergraduate Initial Teacher Education course in Digital Technologies within a Bachelor of Education (Secondary) programme. Drawing on distributed cognition, constructivism, cognitive load theory, and critical AI literacy, the intervention embedded personalised GPT agents within a university Canvas Learning Management System. Fourteen students configured and used agents aligned to curriculum goals, teaching contexts, pedagogical preferences, and weekly Prompt–Reflect–Refine tasks. Data included approximately 7,000 AI interactions, reflective journals, assessed lesson and assessment artefacts, and tutorial-group discussions. A hybrid inductive–deductive thematic analysis identified four recurrent functions in students’ use of the agents: conceptual tutor, co-designer, reflective mirror, and cognitive challenger. Across data sources, students reported clearer conceptual support, iterative planning, and reflective prompting, alongside risks of over-reliance, factual drift, and culturally narrow exemplars. The study contributes a context-specific model for LMS-integrated generative AI that foregrounds partnership, personalisation, judgement, and ethical reflexivity. Findings should be interpreted cautiously because the study was small-scale, single-site, and partly reliant on self-reported reflection.

items.title: Generative AI Decision Support in B2C E-Commerce: A Consumer Buying Behaviour Framework
items.abstract: Decision making in business-to-consumer (B2C) e-commerce connects company and consumer activities before, during and after purchase, whereas many existing generative artificial intelligence (GAI) applications focus on specific tasks or functions. This article develops a conceptual framework linking employee responsibilities, consumer choices, GAI support, information sources, permissions and two-sided evaluation through the five-stage Consumer Buying Behaviour (CBB) process. It connects need clarification, information gathering, feasible-offer comparison, transaction review and post-purchase assessment through decision gates and bounded support functions. Five employees and three consumers participated in a fixed-order ChatGPT 5.6 demonstration to examine the administration and perceived value of the proposed decision-support approach. Following a brief GAI introduction, participants observed ordinary prompt-response support and then a structured CBB-guided sequence within the same general e-commerce decision context. Questionnaire ratings were generally more favourable following CBB guidance, particularly for perceived comparison support and mental effort. The study-specific items are descriptive indicators, and fixed ordering confounds condition with practice, familiarity, novelty, fatigue, expectancy and task-set effects. The contribution is strictly conceptual and methodological; the eight-participant exercise supplies procedural illustration and design input, without establishing effectiveness, deployment readiness or validated system behaviour. Future evaluation requires an implemented system, versioned tasks and outputs, independently scored task-level records, and randomised or counterbalanced comparison.
